before.name: Question 1
before.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
before.html:
Question 1
?

{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=6y(t) Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?

a
b
c
d
e
Submit

decision.explanation: The solutions are x(t)=x(0)e^{6t} and y(t)=y(0)e^{6t}, so every nonzero trajectory is a straight ray directed away from the origin. Option c shows these outward straight trajectories; e has curved trajectories and the other options point inward.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/404c1f68f360e2916a6281033c8a7e9771b648c61156da903ce2f66b931b924e.png)

Writing our system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[6006]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are λ1=λ2=6 with the corresponding eigenvectors [10] and [01].

The general solution of the system is x(t)=c1e6t[10]+c2e6t[01]=e6t[c1c2],c1,c2∈R.

Notice that for each vector [c1c2], we get the straight-line solutions of the form e6t[c1c2] that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector [c1c2].

Since e6t→∞ as t→∞, these solutions move away from the origin as t→∞.

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

before.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[3,\text{ }3]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }3]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/6ec9eac46644188b8b41a1a7ea28ca0542ee7e5c69d713028481904e90dd557a.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.20$ | $0$ | {{field-7}} |
| $y$ | $0.20$ | $3$ | {{field-8}} |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/b0be26a1544bbb3117afab15d004bafee70d831fffab4b1f6921870871ac4768.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/64e685f4ea06a8f497ddfbe50a092a0362b8c92a9d2f78f9da2a8164113a785a.png)
before.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =4,\,v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/6ec9eac46644188b8b41a1a7ea28ca0542ee7e5c69d713028481904e90dd557a.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3t{e}^{4t} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.20$ | $0$ | $0.45$ |
| $y$ | $0.20$ | $3$ | $4.92$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/b0be26a1544bbb3117afab15d004bafee70d831fffab4b1f6921870871ac4768.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/64e685f4ea06a8f497ddfbe50a092a0362b8c92a9d2f78f9da2a8164113a785a.png)

observation.name: Question 2
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[3,\text{ }3]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }3]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

observation.name: Question 2
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[3,\text{ }3]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }3]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/6ec9eac46644188b8b41a1a7ea28ca0542ee7e5c69d713028481904e90dd557a.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

The eigenvector $v=[3,\text{ }3]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }3]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

observation.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =4,\,v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/6ec9eac46644188b8b41a1a7ea28ca0542ee7e5c69d713028481904e90dd557a.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3t{e}^{4t} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.20$ | $0$ | $0.45$ |
| $y$ | $0.20$ | $3$ | $4.92$ |

When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.20$ | $0$ | {{field-7}} |
| $y$ | $0.20$ | $3$ | {{field-8}} |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =4,\,v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3t \\ 3t+3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3t{e}^{4t} \\ y=3(t+1){e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.20$ | $0$ | $0.45$ |
| $y$ | $0.20$ | $3$ | $4.92$ |

observation.name: Question 3
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[1,\text{ }2]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/558ff2994d715139bde11747fdffddbbbd20f17f80c8deb3b90f4ae76078bdba.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=(2t+1){e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

observation.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =-3,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/558ff2994d715139bde11747fdffddbbbd20f17f80c8deb3b90f4ae76078bdba.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-3t} \\ y=(2t+1){e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $y$ | $0.00$ | $1$ | $0.45$ |

${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=(2t+1){e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/c227e135e04b76f093d8c2ad6e2a4365e206c19b281f1a3df7a4b65dd479f411.png)
after.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =-3,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074380/assets/558ff2994d715139bde11747fdffddbbbd20f17f80c8deb3b90f4ae76078bdba.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-3t} \\ y=(2t+1){e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-2.24$ | $0$ | $0.11$ |
| $y$ | $0.00$ | $1$ | $0.45$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[1,\text{ }2]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 2t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to $

{{field-5}}
